posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Why Reasoning Models Think Longer
posts.subtitle: Scaling parameters hit diminishing returns. Scaling how long a model thinks before answering turned out to be a second dial.
posts.summary: Test-time compute means spending extra inference-time work — longer chains of thought, multiple sampled attempts, self-checking — to get a better answer from the same trained model, instead of training a bigger one. It trades latency and cost for accuracy on hard reasoning tasks, and it plateaus: past a point, more thinking stops helping and can even hurt.

slides.title: Two Ways to Make a Model Smarter: Train Bigger, or Think Longer
slides.body: For years, 'scale' meant more parameters and more training data. Reasoning models added a second axis: spend more compute per answer, at inference time, using the exact same weights.
bullets: Train-time scaling: bigger model, more data, higher training cost, fixed inference cost
Test-time scaling: same model, variable inference cost, spent per-question

slides.title: Bigger Models Hit Diminishing Returns — And a Hard Cost Wall
slides.body: Each jump in model scale costs enormously more to train, and the gains on hard reasoning tasks (multi-step math, complex code) started flattening relative to that cost.
bullets: A model that's great at next-token prediction isn't automatically great at 20-step reasoning — fluency and correctness are different axes
Training a bigger model to fix this means months of compute, committed before you know if it'll work
Meanwhile most questions a model answers don't need that extra capacity at all

slides.title: The Core Idea: Spend Compute Per-Question, Not Per-Model
slides.body: Instead of baking more capability into the weights, let the model use more compute on the specific question in front of it, right now.
bullets: Longer chains of thought: the model writes out intermediate reasoning steps before committing to an answer
Sampling multiple attempts: generate several independent reasoning paths, then pick the most common answer (self-consistency / majority voting)
Search-based methods: explore a tree of partial solutions and prune the weak branches (best-of-N, tree-of-thought style search)
A verifier or reward model can score candidate answers and select among them instead of just taking the first one

slides.title: What's Actually Happening Under the Hood
slides.body: In practice, a 'reasoning model' is the same transformer, run with a different decoding strategy and a budget.
bullets: A reasoning budget (max tokens, or max parallel samples) is set per request — easy mode gets a short budget, hard mode gets a long one
Reasoning tokens are often generated in a separate pass or hidden scratchpad before the final answer is produced
A stopping rule decides when to cut off reasoning — fixed token budget, confidence threshold, or diminishing marginal improvement across samples
None of this touches the model's weights — it's entirely a decoding-time choice, swappable per request

slides.title: A Multi-Step Word Problem, Two Ways
slides.body: Ask a model: "A train leaves at 2pm going 60mph, a second leaves 40 minutes later going 75mph on the same track — when does the second catch the first?"
bullets: Low test-time compute: model pattern-matches to a similar-looking problem template and can lock in an early arithmetic slip
High test-time compute: model lays out each leg of the computation as a separate step, checks units, and — critically — can sample the problem several times and keep the answer most paths agree on
The underlying weights are identical in both cases; only the amount of 'thinking' before answering differs

slides.title: Train-Time Scaling vs. Test-Time Scaling

rows: Every single query, proportional to difficulty
New model needed to raise it further
Plateaus — more samples/steps stop helping past a point

slides.title: Where It Breaks Down
slides.body: More thinking isn't free, and it isn't always better.
bullets: Cost and latency scale with how long the model thinks — fine for a hard proof, bad for a chat app's autocomplete
Overthinking is real: past a point, extra reasoning steps can introduce new errors instead of catching old ones
It amplifies reasoning depth, not raw knowledge — a model that doesn't know a fact won't discover it by thinking longer
Self-consistency across samples only helps if the model's errors are somewhat independent between samples; a systematic blind spot survives majority voting unchanged

slides.title: A Second Knob, Not a Replacement for the First
bullets: Test-time compute lets the same trained model trade latency/cost for accuracy, decided per request
Mechanisms: longer chains of thought, multiple sampled paths + majority vote, tree/best-of-N search, verifier-guided selection
It shines on hard, multi-step reasoning tasks and is wasted on easy, fact-lookup ones — route by difficulty, not blanket-apply it
It has a ceiling: past some budget, more thinking yields flat or even negative returns, so unlimited reasoning budget isn't the answer either

questions.prompt: What does "test-time compute" actually scale, compared to training a bigger model?
options: The number of parameters in the model
The amount of inference-time work (reasoning tokens or sampled attempts) spent on a single question
The size of the training dataset
The number of GPUs used during training
questions.explanation: Test-time compute leaves the trained weights untouched and instead spends more inference-time work — longer reasoning chains, more sampled attempts — on the specific question being asked right now.

questions.prompt: Why does self-consistency (sampling multiple reasoning paths and taking the majority answer) have a limit?
options: It only works with temperature set to zero
If the model has a systematic blind spot, most samples will share the same error, so majority voting won't catch it
It requires retraining the model after each sample
It can only be used on classification tasks
questions.explanation: Majority voting across samples helps when errors are roughly independent across attempts. A systematic gap in the model's knowledge or reasoning tends to show up the same way in most samples, so voting doesn't fix it.

questions.prompt: Which task is the worst fit for spending heavy test-time compute?
options: A 20-step competition math proof
A simple factual lookup or short autocomplete where low latency matters
A hard multi-step coding problem
A problem where the model's first few attempts disagree with each other
questions.explanation: Test-time compute trades latency and cost for accuracy on hard reasoning. For simple, low-stakes queries where speed matters, that extra spend buys little benefit and actively hurts the user experience.

posts.title: GraphRAG: When Retrieval Needs the Whole Picture
posts.subtitle: Vector search finds the right chunk. It can't summarize across all of them.
posts.summary: GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from your documents, clusters it into communities, and summarizes each one — so it can answer corpus-wide "what are the themes" questions that top-k chunk retrieval structurally cannot. The cost is a much heavier, pricier indexing pipeline, so it's a tool for specific query shapes, not a universal RAG upgrade.

slides.title: Chunks Answer Questions. They Don't Summarize Corpora.
slides.body: Standard RAG retrieves the top-k chunks most similar to your query and hands them to the LLM. GraphRAG instead builds a knowledge graph of the whole corpus first, so it can answer questions no single chunk ever could.
bullets: Microsoft Research, 2024 — open-sourced as microsoft/graphrag
Trades heavier indexing for corpus-wide reasoning

slides.title: "What Are the Main Themes?" Breaks Top-k Retrieval
slides.body: Vector RAG works by finding chunks whose embeddings are close to the query's embedding. That's great for "what does clause 9 say" — terrible for questions whose answer is spread across hundreds of chunks with no single chunk stating it.
bullets: Ask "what are the recurring risk patterns across 500 contracts" — no chunk contains that sentence
Top-k similarity search has nothing to retrieve, because the answer is emergent, not local
Bigger k doesn't fix it: the LLM just drowns in disconnected fragments

slides.title: Build the Graph First, Summarize It Bottom-Up
slides.body: GraphRAG's indexing pipeline runs once, offline, before any query: extract, cluster, summarize.
bullets: LLM pass 1: extract entities and relationships from every chunk → builds a knowledge graph
Community detection (the Leiden algorithm) clusters tightly-connected entities into hierarchical groups
LLM pass 2: summarize each community, starting at the leaves and rolling summaries up to parent communities
Result: a new queryable layer — community summaries — sitting on top of the raw graph

slides.title: Two Query Modes, Two Very Different Jobs
slides.body: GraphRAG doesn't replace vector search — it adds a second retrieval path for a different question shape.
bullets: Local search: start from entities named in the query, walk their neighborhood in the graph → good for specific, entity-centered questions
Global search: map-reduce over community summaries — ask each community for a partial answer, then synthesize → good for broad, thematic questions
The query itself decides which path fires; global search is the one plain RAG can't replicate

slides.title: A Legal Team, 500 Contracts, Two Questions
slides.body: "What's the termination clause in contract #42?" is a local, factual lookup — plain vector RAG nails it, no graph needed.
bullets: "What are the three most common risk patterns across all 500 contracts?" has no single source chunk
Vector RAG retrieves 10 semi-relevant clauses and the LLM guesses at a pattern from a biased sample
GraphRAG's global search instead map-reduces over every community summary in the corpus, then synthesizes — it's structurally seeing all 500 contracts, not a sample of them

slides.title: Vector RAG vs. GraphRAG

rows: Multiple LLM passes: extraction + per-community summarization
Thematic, corpus-wide ("what are the patterns across X")
Expensive to refresh — new docs can shift community structure
Misses answers synthesized across many chunks
Overkill, slow, and costly for simple lookups

slides.title: Reach for It When the Question Is Bigger Than Any Chunk
bullets: GraphRAG's edge: LLM-built knowledge graph → Leiden community clusters → bottom-up summaries → map-reduce global search
It answers "what are the themes/risks/patterns across this whole corpus" — questions vector RAG structurally can't
It costs real money and time to build and keep fresh, and extraction quality bounds graph quality

Reserve it for large, relatively static corpora where holistic synthesis matters — due diligence, investigative research, enterprise knowledge bases; use plain or hybrid vector RAG for everything else

questions.prompt: What actually lets GraphRAG's "global search" answer thematic questions that stump plain vector RAG?
options: A larger embedding model with more dimensions
Retrieving a much larger value of k
Map-reducing over LLM-generated summaries of entity communities detected in a knowledge graph
Skipping the LLM and querying the graph database directly
questions.explanation: Global search doesn't retrieve raw chunks at all — it asks every community summary for a partial answer, then synthesizes across them. That's what lets it see the whole corpus instead of a sampled slice of it.

questions.prompt: Why does GraphRAG run a community detection algorithm like Leiden on the extracted graph?
options: To rank documents by how often they're retrieved
To group tightly-connected entities into clusters so each cluster can be summarized once, not per-chunk
To compress the embedding vectors for faster search
To remove duplicate documents from the corpus
questions.explanation: Without clustering, you'd need to summarize relationships between every entity pair — intractable at scale. Community detection turns the graph into a manageable hierarchy of groups, each summarized once.

questions.prompt: What's the main practical cost of choosing GraphRAG over plain vector RAG?
options: It can no longer answer specific, factual questions
It requires several extra LLM passes to build and refresh the graph and community summaries, making indexing slower and costlier
It only works on structured tabular data, not text
It removes the need for any LLM at query time
questions.explanation: Plain vector RAG indexes with one embedding pass per chunk. GraphRAG adds an entity/relationship extraction pass plus a summarization pass per community — real compute cost that has to be repaid every time the corpus changes.

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: Splitting the Difference
posts.subtitle: How Llama 2 and Mistral cut KV cache 8x without losing quality
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention sits between full multi-head attention and multi-query attention, letting groups of query heads share a single key/value head. It's the default in Llama 2/3, Mistral, and Qwen because it cuts KV cache memory sharply while keeping almost all of MHA's quality.

slides.title: Three Ways to Split Attention Heads
slides.body: Multi-head attention gives every head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention gives every head the same ones. Grouped-query attention is the tunable middle ground almost every open LLM now ships with.
bullets: MHA: full quality, full memory cost
MQA: ~N× smaller cache, noticeable quality loss
GQA: pick the group size, trade memory for quality on a dial

slides.title: The KV Cache, Not the Weights, Runs Out of Memory First
slides.body: During autoregressive decoding, every attention head must keep a key and value vector cached for every previous token. That cache grows with layers × heads × sequence length × batch size — independent of how many parameters the model has.
bullets: Llama 2 70B: 80 layers, originally 64 attention heads, head_dim 128
With full MHA, a 70B model's KV cache can exceed the size of the model weights at long context + large batch
Bigger cache means fewer concurrent requests and shorter context fit on the same GPU

slides.title: Share Keys and Values Across a Group of Query Heads
slides.body: GQA keeps the full count of query heads (so the model still 'looks' at the sequence from many angles) but shrinks the number of distinct key/value heads, grouping several query heads onto each shared KV head.
bullets: Llama 2 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads for 64 query heads → group size 8
Mistral 7B uses 8 KV heads for 32 query heads → group size 4
MQA is GQA's extreme case: 1 KV head shared by every query head
MHA is the other extreme: group size 1 (no sharing at all)

slides.title: You Don't Have to Retrain From Scratch to Switch
slides.body: The original GQA paper (Ainslie et al., 2023) introduced 'uptraining': take an existing MHA checkpoint, mean-pool each group's key/value heads into one shared head, then fine-tune briefly on a small fraction of the original pretraining data.
bullets: Uptraining typically uses ~5% of original pretraining compute to recover most of the quality lost from merging heads
This is why GQA could be retrofitted onto architectures originally trained with MHA, not just designed in from day one

slides.title: Worked Example: Serving 70B at Long Context
slides.body: KV cache size scales as 2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × batch. Shrinking kv_heads from 64 to 8 shrinks that whole term by 8x.
bullets: At a 32K-token context and a modest batch, an 8x smaller KV cache is the difference between fitting on one GPU and needing to shard just for cache space
That freed memory converts directly into either more concurrent users or longer context windows on the same hardware
Compute cost (FLOPs for attention) barely changes — this is a memory optimization, not a speed-of-math one

slides.title: Where Each Variant Lands
When to Reach for Which Variant
slides.body: GQA won because it's a single hyperparameter — the number of KV head groups — that lets teams dial memory savings against quality loss without a fundamentally new mechanism.
bullets: Training a model from scratch at small scale where memory isn't the bottleneck → plain MHA is simplest
Serving at scale with long context and many concurrent users → GQA with group size 4-8 is the standard default today
Pushing memory to the absolute floor on edge hardware → MQA, accepting the quality hit
Group size is fixed at pretraining (or uptraining) time — you can't change it post-hoc without retraining

questions.prompt: What resource does Grouped-Query Attention primarily save?
options: Total parameter count
KV cache memory during inference
Training dataset size
Tokenizer vocabulary size
questions.explanation: GQA doesn't shrink the model's parameters in any major way — it shrinks how many distinct key/value vectors must be cached per token during decoding, which is what actually limits context length and batch size in production serving.

questions.prompt: A model has 64 query heads and uses GQA with 8 KV heads. How many query heads share each KV head?
questions.explanation: Group size = query heads ÷ KV heads = 64 ÷ 8 = 8. Each shared key/value head serves 8 query heads.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between MQA and GQA?
options: MQA uses more KV heads than any GQA configuration
MQA is the extreme case of GQA where there is exactly 1 KV head
GQA always produces a larger KV cache than MHA
MQA and MHA are the same mechanism with different names
questions.explanation: GQA is a spectrum: group size 1 is plain MHA (no sharing), and group size equal to the total head count is MQA (every head shares one KV head). GQA configurations sit strictly between those two extremes.

posts.title: Reranking: Retrieval Gets You Close, This Gets You Right
posts.subtitle: Why production RAG adds a slower, smarter second pass after vector search
posts.summary: Vector search is fast because it embeds queries and documents independently, but that same independence means it misses relevance signals that only show up when a model reads the query and document together. Cross-encoder reranking fixes the ordering of a small candidate set at the cost of extra latency.

slides.title: Fast Retrieval, Then a Slower Second Opinion
slides.body: Almost every production RAG pipeline that matters runs two passes: a cheap vector search over the whole corpus, then an expensive reranker over just the top candidates.
bullets: Pass 1 (bi-encoder + ANN index): scans millions of chunks in milliseconds
Pass 2 (cross-encoder reranker): re-scores dozens of candidates, fixing order mistakes pass 1 made

slides.title: Bi-Encoders Never Actually Look at Query and Document Together
slides.body: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document independently, then compares vectors with cosine or dot-product similarity. That independence is exactly what makes precomputing and indexing millions of document embeddings possible.
bullets: Because the model never sees the query and document side by side, it can miss negation, exact entity matches, and specific numbers
In practice, the top-20 results from pure vector search often bury 2-3 truly relevant chunks below less relevant ones that just happen to sit nearby in embedding space

slides.title: Cross-Encoders Score the Pair Directly
slides.body: A cross-encoder concatenates the query and a candidate document into one input sequence and runs it through a single transformer, letting attention flow freely between query tokens and document tokens.
bullets: Output is one relevance score per (query, document) pair, not a pair of independent vectors
This catches signals a bi-encoder's separate embeddings can't: exact phrase overlap, negation ('not FDA approved' vs 'FDA approved'), numeric precision
The cost: a fresh forward pass is needed for every pair, every query — nothing about it can be precomputed and stored like embeddings can

slides.title: Inside a Cross-Encoder
slides.body: Typical rerankers (MS MARCO MiniLM-style, BGE-reranker, Cohere Rerank) are smaller transformers — tens to a few hundred million parameters — fine-tuned specifically to output a relevance score from a [query, SEP, document] input, usually via a classification head on the pooled output.
bullets: Small size keeps the per-pair latency low enough to score dozens of candidates in one request
Newer listwise/LLM-based rerankers score or rank a whole candidate list at once instead of pair-by-pair, trading more latency for better calibration across the list

slides.title: Worked Example: A Support-Ticket RAG Pipeline
slides.body: A help-desk assistant embeds a user's question and retrieves the top 50 candidate chunks from a vector index in a few milliseconds.
bullets: The cross-encoder reranker then scores all 50 query-chunk pairs, a step that takes on the order of a few hundred milliseconds
The single most relevant chunk — which raw vector similarity had ranked #18 because it used different wording — moves to #1
Only the reranked top 5 are passed into the LLM's context, directly reducing the chance it answers from a near-miss chunk instead of the right one

slides.title: Two Very Different Jobs

rows: Cheaply find a plausible candidate set
Precisely order that shortlist before it reaches the LLM

slides.title: When Reranking Earns Its Latency Cost — And When It Doesn't
slides.body: Reranking is a precision tool, not a free upgrade: it adds a model call and real latency, so it pays off most when retrieval is the thing failing.
bullets: Skip it when the candidate pool is already tiny and clean (searching <20 documents total), or when the latency budget is sub-100ms
Add it when the corpus is large, phrasing varies a lot between queries and documents, or you've observed the right chunk showing up just outside the top results
A general-purpose reranker trained on web/MS MARCO data may underperform on narrow domains (legal, medical) without domain fine-tuning
Reranking fixes ordering within a candidate set — it can't recover a relevant document that retrieval missed entirely

questions.prompt: Why can't a cross-encoder be used to search millions of documents directly, the way a vector index does?
options: Cross-encoders can only output embeddings, not scores
It must process every query-document pair jointly at query time, so cost scales with corpus size instead of being precomputed
Cross-encoders cannot run on GPUs
Cross-encoders only work with single-word queries
questions.explanation: Bi-encoder embeddings can be computed once per document and indexed for fast lookup later. A cross-encoder needs the specific query present at scoring time, so there's nothing to precompute — running it over an entire corpus per query would be far too slow.

questions.prompt: What can a cross-encoder 'see' that a bi-encoder's separate embeddings cannot?
options: The document's publication date
Direct attention between query tokens and document tokens in the same forward pass
The total length of the corpus
The embedding model's training data
questions.explanation: Because the query and document are fed in together, self-attention lets every query token attend to every document token directly — catching things like negation or exact phrase matches that two independently-computed vectors can lose.

questions.prompt: In a typical two-stage pipeline, what's a realistic shape for the two passes?
options: Retrieve top 2 candidates, then rerank all of them
Retrieve top 50-100 candidates via vector search, then rerank down to the top 5-10
Rerank the whole corpus, then retrieve from the reranked list
Run retrieval and reranking in parallel on the full corpus
questions.explanation: Retrieval's job is to cheaply narrow millions of documents down to a manageable shortlist; reranking's job is to carefully re-order that shortlist. Reversing the order, or reranking the full corpus, defeats the point of having a fast first stage.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Sees
posts.subtitle: Prompting was never the whole game — the full token budget is.
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of curating the full set of tokens an LLM sees at inference time — not just the initial prompt. As agents run longer and accumulate tool outputs, techniques like compaction, structured note-taking, and sub-agent architectures become the real lever on performance, because bigger context windows don't fix 'context rot.'

slides.title: The layer after prompt engineering
slides.body: Anthropic defines context simply: the set of tokens included when sampling from a model. Context engineering is curating the best possible set of those tokens, every single turn an agent runs.
bullets: Prompt engineering writes the instructions; context engineering curates everything the model sees — instructions, tool outputs, memory, retrieved docs
The guiding principle: find the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that makes the desired outcome most likely

slides.title: Context rot: more tokens, less recall
slides.body: A bigger context window doesn't mean the model uses all of it equally well.
bullets: As token count grows, a model's accuracy at recalling specific information from its context declines — shown across needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks on every model tested, though the rate varies
Attention is architecturally a budget: transformers let every token attend to every other token, creating n² pairwise relationships for n tokens — so each new token has diminishing marginal returns
Models also see far less long-sequence training data than short-sequence data, so they're inherently less practiced at using distant context

slides.title: Right-altitude prompts, lean tools
slides.body: The fix starts before the agent even runs: how the system prompt and tools are built.
bullets: 'Right altitude': avoid brittle hardcoded if-else logic on one end and vague guidance that assumes shared context on the other
Structure prompts into clear sections with XML tags or Markdown headers (e.g. <background_information>, <instructions>) rather than one wall of text
Test a minimal prompt on the strongest available model first, then add instructions only in response to observed failure modes — not speculatively
Tools should be self-contained with minimal overlap: if a human engineer can't tell which tool to call, the agent can't either

slides.title: Compaction: summarize, then keep going
slides.body: For long, conversational agent runs, compaction is the primary tool for staying under budget.
bullets: When nearing the context limit, summarize the conversation and start a fresh context window seeded with that summary
Claude Code's version keeps architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details — and discards redundant tool outputs, while keeping the 5 most recently touched files
Tune for recall first (never lose something relevant), then precision (trim what's left)
The lightest form is 'tool result clearing' — stripping raw tool outputs buried deep in history while leaving the rest of the transcript intact

slides.title: Structured notes and sub-agents
slides.body: Two more patterns for runs that outlast a single context window entirely.
bullets: Agents write persistent notes outside the context window and reload them later — Claude Code's to-do list, or a custom agent's NOTES.md file
In one documented case, Claude tracked 1,234 steps of Pokémon training progress across a multi-hour session, resuming correctly after multiple context resets

Sub-agent pattern: a lead agent holds the high-level plan while specialized sub-agents explore in their own clean context windows, each burning tens of thousands of tokens but returning only a distilled 1,000-2,000-token summary

slides.title: Matching the technique to the task
bullets: None of these are free — each adds engineering complexity, so pick based on the shape of the task

rows: Complex research where parallel exploration pays off
Large, dynamic data where pre-loading everything wastes budget

slides.title: Just-in-time beats pre-loading the whole repo
slides.body: Claude Code doesn't embed an entire codebase before answering a question about it.
bullets: Traditional RAG embeds and retrieves relevant chunks before inference even starts
Just-in-time retrieval keeps lightweight pointers — file paths, queries, links — and loads actual data at runtime using tools like glob, grep, head, and tail
Even metadata is a signal: a file named test_utils.py living under tests/ implies a different purpose than one under src/core_logic/
Hybrid works too: Claude Code preloads CLAUDE.md files up front, then retrieves everything else just-in-time — useful when some context is reliably relevant and the rest isn't

slides.title: The core idea in four facts
bullets: Context is every token the model sees, not just the prompt — and bigger context windows don't cancel out context rot
The target is always the smallest set of high-signal tokens, not the largest context you can fit
Compaction, structured note-taking, and sub-agents solve different problems — picking the wrong one adds complexity without fixing recall
Default advice still holds: do the simplest thing that works, and add machinery only once a real failure mode shows up

questions.prompt: What is "context rot"?
options: A bug that corrupts an LLM's weights over time
The tendency for a model's recall accuracy to decline as the number of tokens in its context grows, even within its supported window
A term for outdated training data
A memory leak in agent frameworks
questions.explanation: Context rot describes recall accuracy degrading as token count rises — observed across models on needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks, even though the context technically fits within the model's window.

questions.prompt: In Claude Code's compaction approach, what happens when the context limit approaches?
options: The oldest half of the conversation is deleted at random
The conversation is summarized, keeping architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details plus the 5 most recently touched files, while discarding redundant tool outputs
The agent stops and asks the user to start a new session
All tool outputs are kept but the system prompt is dropped
questions.explanation: Compaction summarizes the conversation before restarting, deliberately preserving architectural decisions, open bugs, and implementation details plus the 5 most recent files — not a random or total truncation.

questions.prompt: According to the guidance, when is a multi-agent (sub-agent) architecture the right call?
options: For every agent task, by default, since more agents is always better
For complex research tasks where parallel exploration across clean context windows pays off
Only when a single agent has exceeded its token budget by a factor of 10
Never — sub-agents are purely experimental
questions.explanation: Sub-agents trade setup complexity for parallel exploration in clean contexts, each returning a distilled summary — a good fit for complex research, not a default for simple iterative tasks where note-taking or compaction suffice.

posts.title: Anthropic's OSS Scanner: Claude Finds Bugs in Open Source for Free
posts.subtitle: A free, opt-in service scans enrolled open-source projects with frontier Claude models and ships a proof of concept with every finding.
posts.summary: Anthropic launched the Cyber Mission on October 8, 2026 — a two-track effort pairing a Critical Infrastructure Defense Program for operational-technology defenders with OSS Scanner, a free service that uses frontier Claude models to scan enrolled open-source projects and return a proof of concept, explanation, and suggested fix for each vulnerability found. Anthropic is targeting a true-positive rate above 90% and warns reports ship without human review.

slides.title: Anthropic turns Claude loose on open-source vulnerabilities, for free
slides.body: The Anthropic Cyber Mission, announced October 8, 2026, is a long-term effort to arm defenders with Claude-powered tools — starting with critical infrastructure and open-source software.
bullets: Two founding tracks: Critical Infrastructure Defense Program (CIDP) and OSS Scanner
OSS Scanner is opt-in and free for enrolled open-source projects

slides.title: Finding a bug and fixing it are months apart
slides.body: Anthropic's own pilot, Project Glasswing, scanned hundreds of widely used open-source projects with human triage of the findings — and the gap between discovery and patch was the real bottleneck.
bullets: Months typically pass between a vulnerability being found and actually fixed, per Anthropic's Glasswing data
Operational-technology (OT) fixes — power grids, water systems, transportation — can take even longer, in rare cases decades
Most open-source maintainers have no dedicated security budget to run this triage themselves

slides.title: OSS Scanner: periodic scans, a PoC, and a suggested fix
slides.body: Enrolled open-source projects get periodic scans from Anthropic's most capable models. Each report bundles a proof of concept, a plain explanation of the bug, and a suggested fix where one is available.
bullets: Opt-in and free — funded in part by the Defender Advantage Fund (0xDAF), launched in August to keep it that way
Reports are sent straight to maintainers without human review first
Anthropic is targeting a true-positive rate above 90%, with plans to keep improving it

slides.title: The other track: trusted access for critical-infrastructure defenders
slides.body: CIDP gives vetted security providers frontier Claude access, on-site Anthropic engineers, and Anthropic's own threat research — aimed at operational technology and government systems.
bullets: Eleven founding partners: Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation
Several partners are already using Claude to fix real vulnerabilities, per Anthropic
Since a June program for state/local/tribal/territorial governments, Claude has been offered to more than half of US states and some large public infrastructure operators

slides.title: What a maintainer actually receives
slides.body: Imagine a mid-size open-source HTTP library enrolled in OSS Scanner.
bullets: Weekly automated scan flags a path-traversal bug in a file-upload handler introduced three commits ago
The report includes a working proof-of-concept request that triggers the bug, a plain-English explanation of why the path check is insufficient, and a suggested patch
The maintainer merges the fix the same day — instead of the months-long discovery-to-patch gap Glasswing measured industry-wide

slides.title: CIDP vs. OSS Scanner: two tracks, two audiences
bullets: Same underlying models and threat research, aimed at very different defenders

rows: Vetted security providers protecting OT/government systems
Automated periodic scans, no human review
Hundreds of projects scanned under Project Glasswing

slides.title: Why Anthropic is flagging its own limits
slides.body: The announcement is unusually candid about where this can go wrong.
bullets: Reports go out without human review, so some will have errors — Anthropic specifically calls out wrong severity ratings as a known failure mode
Anthropic's own forecast: AI likely favors defenders more in about two years, but the near term may not clearly favor either side
A free, automated scanner that misjudges severity could still waste maintainer time chasing a false 'critical' — the tradeoff for catching real bugs faster

slides.title: The core idea in four facts
bullets: Anthropic's Cyber Mission (Oct 8, 2026) pairs CIDP for critical infrastructure with a free OSS Scanner for open-source projects
OSS Scanner reports include a proof of concept, explanation, and suggested fix — unreviewed by humans before they reach maintainers
Anthropic targets a >90% true-positive rate and plans to automate triage and patching next
The real bottleneck it targets isn't finding bugs — Glasswing showed the fix can take months, or decades for OT systems

questions.prompt: What does every OSS Scanner report include alongside a flagged vulnerability?
options: Only a severity score with no further detail
A proof of concept, a plain-English explanation, and a suggested fix where available
A bug bounty payout
A mandatory code freeze notice
questions.explanation: Anthropic designed OSS Scanner reports to bundle a working proof of concept, an explanation of the bug, and a suggested fix when one exists — aimed at cutting the time from discovery to patch.

questions.prompt: What was the main bottleneck Anthropic's Project Glasswing pilot actually measured?
options: A lack of vulnerabilities to find
The gap between finding a vulnerability and actually getting it fixed, which stretched to months — or decades for OT systems
Open-source maintainers refusing to use AI tools
The cost of running large language models
questions.explanation: Glasswing scanned hundreds of open-source projects and found that discovery wasn't the hard part — the fix lag was, sometimes running to decades for operational-technology systems.

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic explicitly warn that OSS Scanner reports can contain errors like wrong severity ratings?
options: Because the scanner is a beta product not actually in use
Because reports are sent to maintainers without human review before delivery
Because open-source code is inherently unscannable
Because severity ratings are randomly assigned
questions.explanation: OSS Scanner sends its automated reports straight to maintainers without a human review step, so Anthropic flags that some reports — including severity ratings — may be wrong even while targeting a >90% true-positive rate.

posts.title: Product Quantization: Shrinking Billions of Vectors to Fit in RAM
posts.subtitle: Split each vector into subvectors, replace each with the nearest of 256 learned centroids, and cut memory by 32x or more.
posts.summary: Storing raw float32 embeddings for a large corpus gets expensive fast — 100M 768-dim vectors cost over 300GB. Product quantization (PQ) splits each vector into subvectors, replaces each with the ID of its nearest pre-learned centroid, and shrinks that same corpus to under 10GB — at the cost of a small, tunable loss in recall.

slides.title: Why a billion embeddings don't fit in memory
slides.body: A single 768-dimensional float32 embedding costs 3,072 bytes. At 100M vectors, that's over 300GB before you've built any index on top.
bullets: Vector databases keep embeddings in RAM for speed — raw float32 storage doesn't scale
Product quantization (PQ) compresses each vector into a handful of tiny codes, often 32-64x smaller

slides.title: Exact nearest-neighbor search doesn't scale on cost or speed
slides.body: Keeping every vector at full precision means both a huge memory footprint and a full distance computation against every stored vector at query time.
bullets: Memory: 100M x 768-dim float32 vectors = ~307GB, before index overhead
Compute: a brute-force scan is O(n x d) per query — d multiplications per comparison, for every one of n vectors
Scalar quantization (storing each dimension in 1 byte instead of 4) only buys a 4x reduction — not enough at real scale

slides.title: Split into subvectors, quantize each against its own codebook
slides.body: PQ splits a d-dimensional vector into m equal subvectors, then runs k-means separately on each subspace to learn a codebook of k centroids (commonly k=256, so each code fits in 1 byte).
bullets: Each subvector is replaced by the index of its nearest centroid in that subspace's codebook — not the centroid's actual values
A 768-dim vector split into m=96 subvectors of 8 dims each, coded at 1 byte per subvector, stores in just 96 bytes
That's 3,072 bytes -> 96 bytes per vector: a 32x compression ratio, computed directly from the split

slides.title: Distance at query time: precompute, then just add
slides.body: PQ never fully decompresses a stored vector to score it. Instead it precomputes a small distance table once per query.
bullets: For each of the m subspaces, compute the distance from the query's subvector to all k centroids — m x k numbers total (e.g. 96 x 256 = 24,576), computed once per query
Scoring any stored vector is then just m table lookups and an add — no multiplication against the original dimensions at all
In FAISS this is Asymmetric Distance Computation (ADC): the query stays full-precision, only the stored vectors are compressed

slides.title: IVFPQ: pairing PQ with a coarse partition
slides.body: FAISS's IVFPQ index combines an inverted file (IVF) with PQ to avoid scanning the whole compressed corpus on every query.
bullets: Step 1: k-means partitions the corpus into, say, 1,024 coarse buckets at index-build time
Step 2: a query only searches the few nearest buckets (e.g. 8-16 of 1,024), not all of them
Step 3: within those buckets, PQ-compressed residual vectors (the vector minus its bucket centroid) are scored via the distance-table lookup — so compression and partitioning compound
Result: both the scan size and the per-vector cost shrink, not just one of them

slides.title: Flat vs. scalar quantization vs. product quantization
bullets: PQ trades a small, tunable recall hit for a compression ratio nothing else here gets close to

rows: Small-to-moderate loss, tunable via m and k
k-means training per subspace, needs representative data

slides.title: When PQ is the wrong tool
slides.body: Compression isn't free, and PQ's costs show up in specific, predictable places.
bullets: It's lossy: fine-grained similarity distinctions can blur, especially at small m (fewer, coarser subvectors)
Codebooks must be trained on enough representative vectors per centroid — too little training data and the centroids don't generalize
Retraining a codebook is expensive, so PQ fits static or batch-rebuilt indexes far better than corpora with heavy continuous updates
For a small corpus (under a few million vectors) that already fits comfortably in RAM uncompressed, PQ adds build complexity and recall loss for no real benefit

slides.title: The core idea in four facts
bullets: PQ splits each vector into m subvectors and replaces each with a 1-byte centroid ID from a per-subspace codebook
A 768-dim float32 vector (3,072 bytes) compresses to ~96 bytes at m=96 — a 32x reduction
Query-time scoring uses precomputed distance tables (ADC) — table lookups and adds, no per-dimension multiplication
Pair it with IVF (as in FAISS's IVFPQ) to also cut how much of the compressed corpus gets scanned at all

questions.prompt: In product quantization, what does each subvector actually get replaced with?
options: The average of all vectors in the corpus
The index (ID) of its nearest centroid in that subspace's learned codebook
A random 1-byte value
The full original subvector, unchanged
questions.explanation: PQ runs k-means per subspace to learn a codebook of centroids, then stores only the ID of the nearest centroid for each subvector — not any of the original float values.

questions.prompt: A 768-dim float32 vector (3,072 bytes) is split into m=96 subvectors, each coded in 1 byte. What's the resulting compression ratio?
options: 4x
8x
questions.explanation: 96 subvectors at 1 byte each is 96 bytes total. 3,072 / 96 = 32x compression — the direct result of splitting into m=96 pieces and coding each in a single byte.

questions.prompt: Why does PQ avoid fully decompressing stored vectors at query time?
options: It doesn't — full decompression is required before scoring
It precomputes a small per-subspace distance table once per query, then scores stored vectors with table lookups and adds
It skips distance computation entirely and returns random results
It only works if every vector is first converted back to float32
questions.explanation: This is Asymmetric Distance Computation: the query stays full-precision and a query-to-centroid distance table is built once per subspace, so scoring any compressed vector is just cheap lookups and summation.

posts.title: AgentGarten: Code Worlds Built From Simulators, Not Pixels
posts.subtitle: Pair a rule-true simulator with a neural renderer, and an agent's training world can be both correct and photoreal.
posts.summary: MirroS-Lab's AgentGarten (arXiv 2610.12374) proposes 'code worlds': persistent, rule-based simulators paired with a shared neural renderer so an agent's training environment is simultaneously faithful (correct state and rules) and realistic (video-model-quality observations). The renderer — built on Cosmos3-Nano and trained in three stages ending in a distillation step called Adversarial Forcing — is public now; the code worlds and agent practice loop are still marked TODO on the project's GitHub.

slides.title: A training world that is both correct and real-looking
slides.body: AgentGarten (MirroS-Lab, arXiv 2610.12374, Oct 2026) tackles a split that's dogged agent training for years: simulators are rule-correct but look fake; video generators look real but don't enforce any rules. AgentGarten fuses both into a 'code world.'

slides.title: Faithful or realistic — training worlds rarely get both
slides.body: A hand-built game engine enforces consistent physics and state, but its graphics are obviously synthetic. A pure video model can render gorgeous frames, but nothing stops it from hallucinating a door that isn't there or ignoring gravity. Agents trained on either alone learn the wrong lessons.
bullets: Game-engine worlds: correct rules, cheap to run, visually synthetic
Video-model worlds: realistic pixels, but no guaranteed state consistency
AgentGarten's bet: keep the simulator for truth, add a renderer only for pixels

slides.title: The simulator keeps the rules; a shared renderer keeps the pixels
slides.body: A persistent simulator or game engine owns state and program-defined rules, and exports per-frame geometry (depth and surface normals). A single shared neural renderer turns that geometry into the agent's actual visual observation — so the 'world' can be swapped out without retraining a new renderer each time.
bullets: Simulator = ground truth: state, physics, win/loss conditions
Renderer = perception: geometry in, photoreal frame out
One renderer serves many different code worlds

slides.title: The renderer is trained in three stages, fastest-last
slides.body: Each stage solves a different problem: learning the visual distribution, then making it streamable, then making it fast enough for real-time agent interaction.

rows: Bidirectional rectified-flow on full clips from a first frame
Streams frame-by-frame with a KV cache instead of whole clips
Collapses many diffusion steps into a few-step student for real-time use

slides.title: Worked example: one renderer, three different code worlds
slides.body: Picture three simulators — a warehouse-robot sim, a city-traffic sim, and a Linux desktop sim — each exporting depth/normal maps per step. The same trained renderer paints all three into realistic frames. An agent dropped into any of them sees photoreal video, while the underlying simulator still enforces 'you can't walk through a wall' or 'this command actually fails without sudo.'
bullets: Swapping worlds means swapping the simulator, not retraining vision
After each round, agents write up what worked into a playbook the next round inherits
Knowledge compounds across rounds as text, not just as gradient updates

slides.title: What's real today versus what's still a TODO
slides.body: As of the project's October 8, 2026 release, only the perception half is public — the parts that make a 'code world' usable for agent training are explicitly listed as not-yet-released on the GitHub repo.
bullets: Released: renderer training code, streaming inference, serving kernels, the technical report
Not yet released: the real-time rendering engine (server + interactive frontend)
Not yet released: the code worlds themselves and the agent practice loop (play → review → playbook)
Cost tradeoff: every observation now costs a video-model forward pass, not a cheap engine render

slides.title: Decouple 'is this world true' from 'does this world look real'
slides.body: AgentGarten's core idea is architectural, not a single benchmark number: separate correctness (owned by a programmable simulator) from perception (owned by one reusable neural renderer), and let agents accumulate know-how between rounds as written playbooks.
bullets: A simulator guarantees state and rules; a renderer only guarantees pixels
One distilled, few-step renderer can serve many different simulated worlds
Today the renderer ships; the full agent-training loop is still coming

questions.prompt: What is the job of AgentGarten's 'shared neural renderer'?
options: It replaces the simulator's rule logic entirely
It turns the simulator's exported geometry (depth/normals) into realistic visual frames
It computes the agent's reward signal
It stores the agent's playbooks between rounds
questions.explanation: The renderer only handles perception — converting geometry the simulator exports into a realistic frame. The simulator itself still owns state, physics, and rules; the two are deliberately kept separate.

questions.prompt: What does the 'Adversarial Forcing' training stage accomplish?
options: It prevents agents from exploiting the simulator
It distills the slow, multi-step autoregressive renderer into a fast few-step student using a discriminator
It enforces physics rules inside the simulator
It encrypts the playbooks agents write between rounds
questions.explanation: Adversarial Forcing is the third training stage: a real-data discriminator (with R1/R2 regularization) trains a few-step 'student' to match the quality of the slower multi-step autoregressive model, which is what makes real-time streaming possible.

questions.prompt: Per the project's own GitHub README, what was actually public as of October 8, 2026?
options: Everything, including the code worlds and the agent practice loop
Only the neural renderer — its training code and streaming inference; the code worlds and practice loop are still TODO
Only benchmark results, with no code released
Nothing — the repository was still empty
questions.explanation: The README explicitly lists the renderer (training + streaming inference + serving kernels) as released, while the real-time rendering engine, the code worlds, and the agent practice loop are checklist items still marked as TODO.

posts.title: MCP: One Protocol So Any Agent Can Use Any Tool
posts.subtitle: Before MCP, every AI app needed custom glue for every tool. MCP turns that N×M mess into one standard wire format.
posts.summary: The Model Context Protocol standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, data, and prompt templates through a client-server architecture over JSON-RPC. Instead of every agent writing bespoke integration code for every tool, a tool is wrapped once as an MCP server and any MCP-compatible host can use it — at the cost of a new security surface where a malicious server can see every message that reaches it.

slides.title: A USB-C port for connecting agents to tools
slides.body: Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 as an open protocol so AI applications don't each need a one-off integration for every tool and data source they want to use. It's commonly described as a USB-C port for AI apps: one standard connector instead of a custom cable for every app-to-tool pairing.

slides.title: The N×M integration problem
slides.body: Say you have 5 AI apps (Claude Desktop, an IDE assistant, a custom agent, a chatbot, a CLI tool) and 8 tools they might all want (GitHub, Postgres, Slack, a file system, Sentry, Google Drive, a search API, a CRM). Without a shared protocol, that's up to 40 separate hand-written integrations.
bullets: Every app re-implements auth, schema, and error handling per tool
A tool author who wants to reach N different AI apps writes N different adapters
None of that integration code is reusable outside the app it was written for

slides.title: Host, Client, Server — a dedicated connection per tool
slides.body: An MCP Host (e.g. Claude Desktop, an IDE) runs one MCP Client per tool it wants to use. Each client holds a 1:1 connection to one MCP Server, which wraps a specific tool or data source. On connect, the server advertises what it offers; the host doesn't need to know anything about the tool in advance.
bullets: Transport is local (stdio, a subprocess) or remote (Streamable HTTP)
Each server runs independently — one process per tool, not one shared integration layer
The LLM only ever sees the flattened, advertised capability list, not the wire protocol

slides.title: Three primitives, three different controllers
slides.body: MCP servers expose capabilities as one of three primitive types, and each is controlled by a different party — which is the detail most new integrations get wrong.

rows: The model — it chooses to call them
The user — picks a template explicitly

slides.title: Worked example: one coding agent, three servers
slides.body: A coding agent's host opens three MCP clients at session start: a GitHub server (tools: create_issue, list_prs), a Postgres server (resource: read-only schema browser, tool: run_query), and a Sentry server (tool: get_recent_errors). Each server was written once by whoever owns that system — not by the agent's developer.
bullets: The agent decides to call get_recent_errors, then run_query to check if a bad migration caused it
The host routes each call to the right server; the model never sees three different APIs, just one tool list
Swap in a fourth server (e.g. Linear) and the agent gains that capability with zero code changes to the agent itself

slides.title: MCP versus writing the integration yourself
slides.body: The win isn't capability — you could always wire a tool into an agent by hand. The win is who pays the integration cost, and how many times.

rows: New glue code per app × per tool
Written once, by the tool owner

slides.title: When MCP is overkill — and its real security surface
slides.body: A single app talking to one fixed internal API doesn't need a protocol handshake, process management, and capability negotiation — direct function calling is simpler. And every MCP server you add is also new attack surface.
bullets: A local stdio server runs with your host process's permissions — installing a shady community server is close to arbitrary code execution
A server's tool descriptions and results flow straight into the model's context, so a compromised or malicious server can smuggle instructions back to the agent ('tool poisoning')
MCP standardizes the plumbing, not retrieval quality — a resource can still hand the model too much, or irrelevant, context

slides.title: MCP is the plumbing, not the intelligence
slides.body: MCP doesn't make a model smarter at using tools — it standardizes the wire format so a tool integration, written once, works across every compliant AI application.
bullets: Three primitives, three controllers: Tools (model), Resources (app), Prompts (user)
1 client : 1 server, over stdio locally or Streamable HTTP remotely
Only install servers you trust — they see raw context and can act with your host's permissions

questions.prompt: What problem does MCP primarily solve?
options: Making a model reason more accurately
The N×M problem where every AI app needs a custom integration for every tool
Reducing GPU memory usage during inference
Replacing vector databases in a RAG pipeline
questions.explanation: Without a shared protocol, every pairing of app and tool needs its own hand-written adapter. MCP lets a tool be wrapped once, as a server, and used by any MCP-compatible host.

questions.prompt: In MCP's architecture, how do clients and servers relate?
options: One client connects to many servers at once
Each MCP client maintains a dedicated 1:1 connection to one MCP server
Servers connect directly to each other, peer-to-peer
There's no client — the host talks to servers directly
questions.explanation: A host runs a separate client for each server it wants to use; each client-server pair is its own connection, which is what lets servers be added or removed independently.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of MCP's three core primitives?
options: Tools
Resources
Prompts
Weights
questions.explanation: MCP's three primitives are Tools (model-invoked functions), Resources (app-attached context), and Prompts (user-selected templates). Model weights have nothing to do with the protocol — MCP only standardizes how context and actions move between a host and a server.

posts.title: Google's Gemini Agent: One Prompt Box for All of Work
posts.subtitle: A persistent agent that lives in Gmail, Slack, and your terminal — and keeps working after you close the laptop.
posts.summary: Google Cloud announced the Gemini agent on October 8, 2026: a single, persistent agent that answers questions, does knowledge work, creates media, and writes/runs code from one prompt box, choosing between Gemini and Claude models per task. It runs in the cloud with shared memory so multi-day jobs keep going after you log off, and it ships with governance features like cryptographic agent identity and an 'Agent Gateway' policy firewall.

slides.title: One prompt box replaces a dozen specialized tools
slides.body: Announced October 8, 2026 at Gemini at Work 2026, the Gemini agent is Google Cloud's pitch for a single, universal agent for work: it answers questions, does knowledge work, creates images and media, and writes and runs code — all from one interface.

slides.title: You give it objectives, not step-by-step instructions
slides.body: Most AI assistants still need to be walked through a task turn by turn. Google's framing: 'work now starts in the prompt window' — you state the goal, and the agent figures out the steps, inside the tools you already use (Gmail, Docs, Sheets, developer environments).
bullets: Knowledge workers juggle separate chat tools, each scoped to one app
Multi-hour or multi-day tasks don't survive a closed laptop in a typical chatbot
Google's answer: persistence and cloud execution, not a bigger context window

slides.title: Persistent execution with one shared memory
slides.body: The agent runs in the cloud, not in a browser tab, with a shared memory and personalization graph. A multi-hour research task or a multi-day migration keeps running after you close your laptop — you come back to finished work.

It explicitly orchestrates across model vendors — Gemini and Claude — not just Google's own stack

posts.title: LingBot-Map: Streaming 3D Reconstruction Without SLAM
posts.subtitle: A single camera feed becomes a drift-corrected 3D map, frame by frame, with no pose graph in sight.
posts.summary: LingBot-Map replaces classical SLAM's explicit pose graphs and bundle adjustment with a feed-forward transformer that learns geometric reasoning directly in its attention weights. It sustains roughly 20 FPS on sequences over 10,000 frames from a single camera, and it's listed as an ECCV 2026 Best Paper Award candidate.

slides.title: A transformer that reconstructs 3D space as it streams in
slides.body: LingBot-Map (Robbyant team, ECCV 2026 Best Paper Award candidate) turns a live video feed into a running 3D reconstruction — camera poses plus a point cloud — using one feed-forward model instead of a classical SLAM pipeline.

slides.title: Classical SLAM wasn't built for this
slides.body: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) traditionally maintains an explicit pose graph and runs bundle adjustment to correct drift — accurate, but expensive, and real-time performance degrades as the sequence grows. Optimization-based 3D reconstruction methods are even further from real-time: they refine a scene offline rather than streaming.
bullets: Pose graphs and loop closure add latency that compounds over long sequences
Optimization-based reconstruction needs the full sequence before it can refine anything
Error ('drift') accumulates frame over frame with no cheap way to correct it online

slides.title: Geometric reasoning, learned in attention — not bolted on as a graph
slides.body: LingBot-Map's core contribution is the Geometric Context Transformer: three attention components that together replace what a pose graph and bundle adjustment used to do explicitly.
bullets: Anchor context — handles coordinate grounding (where is this frame relative to the world?)
Pose-reference window — supplies dense geometric cues from nearby frames
Trajectory memory — compresses the full history into compact per-frame tokens for long-range drift correction

slides.title: DINO features in, pose and point cloud out
slides.body: A DINO backbone extracts image features per frame; these pass through alternating Frame Attention and Geometric Context Attention (GCA) layers. Because trajectory memory holds a fixed-size compressed token per past frame rather than the raw history, memory and compute per new frame stay nearly constant even past 10,000 frames.
bullets: Trained with video RoPE on 320-view sequences, then run with windowed inference for arbitrarily long streams
Paged, KV-cache-style attention avoids reprocessing the entire past on every new frame
No test-time optimization step — it's a single forward pass per frame

slides.title: Three approaches to the same problem
slides.body: The paper reports outperforming both streaming and optimization-based baselines across benchmarks, without disclosing exact scores in the public materials reviewed here — so this compares mechanisms, not leaderboard numbers.

rows: No — needs the whole video first

slides.title: A single RGB camera, no LiDAR, 10,000+ frames
slides.body: Picture a robot or handheld rig scanning a multi-room building with one ordinary camera. A classical pipeline would need loop closure passes to keep the map consistent as the robot revisits rooms. LingBot-Map instead updates its compressed trajectory memory every frame at ~20 FPS (518×378 resolution), so the pose and point-cloud estimate for frame 10,000 benefits from everything the model has seen since frame 1 — without re-reading frame 1.
bullets: No LiDAR or depth sensor required — monocular RGB input only
Streaming output means downstream robotics code gets usable poses frame by frame, not after the fact

slides.title: Where a feed-forward model is the wrong tool
slides.body: A single forward pass has no explicit error bound the way bundle adjustment does — you can't easily ask it to re-optimize once more for guaranteed global consistency.
bullets: Survey-grade or safety-critical mapping, where a verifiable consistency guarantee matters more than speed, still favors classical bundle adjustment
The model was trained on 320-view windows — sequences with very different structure (e.g. extreme viewpoint jumps) may fall outside what it learned
Public benchmark numbers beyond the ~20 FPS figure weren't available in the materials reviewed, so treat accuracy comparisons as the authors' own claims pending independent verification

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LingBot-Map replaces explicit SLAM machinery (pose graphs, bundle adjustment) with geometry learned inside attention weights
Trajectory memory's fixed-size per-frame tokens are what keep compute roughly constant past 10,000 frames
It's feed-forward and streaming — no test-time optimization, no LiDAR, ~20 FPS on a single camera
A recognized signal of quality (ECCV 2026 Best Paper Award candidate) doesn't substitute for published, independently verified benchmark numbers

questions.prompt: What are the three components of LingBot-Map's Geometric Context Transformer?
options: Anchor context, pose-reference window, trajectory memory
Encoder, decoder, and a pose graph
RGB input, depth sensor, and LiDAR fusion
Bundle adjustment, loop closure, and keyframe selection
questions.explanation: These three attention components handle coordinate grounding, dense geometric cues from nearby frames, and long-range drift correction respectively — together replacing what a classical SLAM pipeline does explicitly.

questions.prompt: Why does LingBot-Map's compute stay roughly constant per frame even past 10,000 frames?
options: It discards all but the last 10 frames
It reprocesses the entire video history on every new frame
Trajectory memory compresses the full history into fixed-size per-frame tokens instead of reprocessing raw history
It runs on specialized LiDAR hardware
questions.explanation: The key efficiency trick is that trajectory memory holds a compact, fixed-size token per past frame rather than raw history — so adding a new frame doesn't make old frames more expensive to account for.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of LingBot-Map's feed-forward approach compared to classical bundle adjustment?
options: It cannot process video at all
It requires expensive LiDAR sensors
It has no explicit error bound or re-optimization step for guaranteed global consistency
It only works on static images
questions.explanation: A single forward pass gives you an estimate, not a verifiable consistency guarantee the way iterative bundle adjustment can — which matters for survey-grade or safety-critical mapping.

posts.title: HNSW: The Graph That Makes Vector Search Fast
posts.subtitle: Skip scanning millions of embeddings — hop through a small-world graph instead.
posts.summary: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs let RAG pipelines find a query's nearest embeddings in roughly logarithmic time instead of scanning every vector. A multi-layer graph with sparse 'highway' links on top and dense local links below lets search start far away and zero in fast — at the cost of memory, approximate (not exact) recall, and awkward deletes.

slides.title: Finding 'nearest' among millions of vectors, fast
slides.body: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithm behind most production vector databases — the index that makes RAG retrieval feel instant instead of scanning everything.

slides.title: Brute-force search doesn't survive scale
slides.body: A flat index compares a query embedding against every stored vector — O(n) work per query. At 50 million chunks, that's 50 million dot products per query, every query, which blows past any RAG latency budget.
bullets: RAG pipelines typically need retrieval in well under 100ms
Flat/brute-force search is exact but doesn't scale past a few hundred thousand vectors in practice
Clustering-based indexes (e.g. IVF) help, but still require a training/clustering pass and can miss neighbors across cluster boundaries

slides.title: A graph with highways on top, side streets below
slides.body: HNSW builds several stacked graph layers, like a skip list generalized to graphs. The top layer is sparse, with long-range links connecting far-apart points — the 'highway.' Lower layers get progressively denser, with only the bottom layer containing every point and its true local neighbors.
bullets: Search starts at the top layer and greedily moves to whichever neighbor is closer to the query
When no closer neighbor exists at that layer, search drops down one layer and keeps refining
By the bottom layer, you're already near the true answer — just a local search away from it

slides.title: Two knobs: M and ef
slides.body: Each point links to its M nearest neighbors per layer (a heuristic keeps those links diverse, not all clustered in one direction — otherwise the graph loses its 'small world' shortcuts). Search quality is tuned with ef (the candidate list size kept while traversing): efConstruction controls build-time quality, efSearch controls query-time recall.
bullets: Higher M and ef → better recall, more memory, slower build and search
New points are assigned a random top layer via an exponentially decaying probability — that's what keeps upper layers sparse
This is an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) method: it trades a small, tunable amount of recall for a large speedup

slides.title: HNSW vs. the alternatives

rows: Inserts are native; deletes usually need tombstoning or a rebuild

slides.title: 50 million chunks, a few hundred comparisons
slides.body: A RAG app indexes 50 million document chunks with HNSW (M=16, efSearch=100). Instead of 50 million comparisons, a query hops through a handful of top-layer nodes, drops down a few layers, and does a local search at the bottom — typically a few hundred distance computations total, returning the top-10 nearest chunks in low single-digit milliseconds.
bullets: The speedup comes from never visiting most of the graph, not from a faster distance function
Recall is tunable: raising efSearch recovers accuracy at the cost of visiting more nodes per query

slides.title: When HNSW is the wrong default
slides.body: HNSW stores the full graph structure (edges at every layer) in memory alongside the vectors themselves — expect noticeably more RAM than the raw embeddings alone, which matters at billion-scale.
bullets: Small datasets (well under ~10k vectors): brute-force is simpler, exact, and often just as fast in wall-clock time
Heavy delete/update workloads: HNSW has no cheap native delete — most implementations tombstone or periodically rebuild
Recall is never guaranteed 100%: an approximate index can miss the true nearest neighbor, which matters for exact-match-sensitive use cases
Memory-constrained environments may prefer IVF or a quantized index over HNSW's graph overhead

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: HNSW turns nearest-neighbor search into a graph traversal: sparse long-range links on top, dense local links at the bottom
M (links per node) and ef (candidate list size) are the recall/speed/memory dials — tune per workload
It's approximate, not exact — a small recall tradeoff buys roughly logarithmic query time
Great default for large, mostly-static embedding sets; reconsider for tiny datasets or delete-heavy workloads

questions.prompt: Why can't a flat (brute-force) index keep up at RAG scale?
options: It only supports text, not embeddings
It requires GPUs that most teams don't have
It compares the query against every stored vector — O(n) work per query
It can only store 1,000 vectors maximum
questions.explanation: Brute-force search is exact precisely because it checks everything — but that O(n) cost per query is what makes it impractical once you're past a few hundred thousand vectors.

questions.prompt: What role do the upper layers play in an HNSW graph?
options: They store a backup copy of all vectors in case of failure
They hold sparse, long-range 'highway' links that let search jump far across the space quickly
They contain only the most recently inserted vectors
They're used exclusively during index deletion
questions.explanation: Upper layers are deliberately sparse and long-range — that's what lets a query starting at the top cover a lot of 'distance' in a few hops before dropping down to refine locally.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of HNSW compared to a flat index?
options: It cannot be used for text embeddings
Search results are approximate — it can miss the true nearest neighbor — and deletes aren't natively cheap
It only works with exactly one distance metric, cosine similarity
It requires retraining on the full dataset for every new insert
questions.explanation: HNSW trades exactness for speed: recall is tunable but never guaranteed at 100%, and because deletion would break the graph's link structure, most implementations tombstone or rebuild rather than delete in place.

posts.title: Claude Finds a New CRISPR-Like System in Bacteriophages
posts.subtitle: 950 agents, 21 hours, 200,000 enzymes scanned — and one repeat pattern a human hadn't flagged.
posts.summary: Anthropic's life sciences group pointed Claude at a massive sequence database to hunt for new reverse transcriptases, and one agent noticed a CRISPR-like repeat array next to an otherwise unremarkable enzyme — a system now called ART. It's a concrete look at agentic science: fast, wide search narrowed hard before any human lab work begins.

slides.title: An AI agent noticed a pattern humans hadn't flagged
slides.body: On September 23, 2026, Anthropic's life sciences research group announced that Claude identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme system — array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ART — while searching a public DNA database for new reverse-transcriptase enzymes.
bullets: Found mainly in bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria)
The repeat array visually resembles a CRISPR array, but ART's function is still unknown
Pre-print reviewer Feng Zhang (MIT/Broad Institute) called it 'an exciting example of how AI agents can contribute to biological discovery'

slides.title: Finding a new biological system is a needle-in-a-haystack problem
slides.body: Public sequence databases hold hundreds of millions of genes. A reverse transcriptase (an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA) can look nearly identical across thousands of unrelated systems, so spotting one with an unusual, meaningful neighbor is slow, expert-hours-intensive work.
bullets: Reverse transcriptases already pair with many diverse accessory systems
Most candidates are minor variants of systems already catalogued
The real signal is rare and buried inside volume, not complexity

slides.title: Scale the search with agents, then narrow hard before any lab work
slides.body: Claude was prompted to search the sequence database for new reverse-transcriptase systems. The agentic search ran for 21 hours using roughly 950 agents and about 210 million tokens.
bullets: Gathered over 200,000 candidate reverse transcriptases
Agents narrowed that pool to 3,500 candidate systems
A final filtering pass kept only the 20 most compelling, each written up as its own report for human review

slides.title: The discovery moment: noticing a repeat by eye
slides.body: While one agent was reading the raw sequence flanking a candidate reverse transcriptase, it noticed a tandem repeat array next to the gene — then counted the repeats, measured their spacing, compared the layout to known systems, and checked the literature before filing the report.
bullets: Claude's own note during analysis: "I can see by eye a tandem repeat array..."
The array is also expressed as a set of distinct short RNAs — a possible, unconfirmed parallel to how CRISPR arrays are processed
Humans then expressed the protein in standard lab strains, at a Bay Area lab working only at BSL-1/2 with no human pathogens

slides.title: ART next to the system it resembles
A pattern match is a lead, not a proof
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit that ART's function is still unknown — the resemblance to CRISPR is structural, not a confirmed mechanism. This is agentic hypothesis-generation at scale, not autonomous discovery: every candidate still needed human lab validation before anyone could call it real.
bullets: Of 3,500 candidate systems, only 20 were judged worth a human look — most agent output is still noise to filter
The lab intentionally works only with non-pathogenic bacteriophage systems at BSL-1/2
The claim rests on a pre-print reviewed by outside experts, not yet independently replicated

slides.title: What this actually demonstrates about agentic science
slides.body: This is one of the first projects from Anthropic's life sciences research group, formed in spring 2026, which pairs Claude Science and Claude Code agents with human biologists at every step.
bullets: Agents are good at tireless, wide-scale pattern search across volumes no human team could read by hand
The valuable moment was still a human-interpretable visual pattern, not a black-box leap
Expect more 'candidate-then-validate' discovery pipelines, not autonomous AI biologists

questions.prompt: How did Anthropic's life sciences group task Claude to search for ART?
options: It was explicitly told to look for CRISPR-like repeats
It was prompted to search a sequence database for new reverse transcriptases, and noticed the repeat array along the way
It was trained specifically on phage genomes
It ran a targeted search against known CRISPR arrays
questions.explanation: Claude wasn't looking for a CRISPR-like system specifically — it was searching broadly for new reverse transcriptases, and the repeat pattern turned up as a side observation while reading the flanking sequence.

questions.prompt: What narrowed 200,000+ candidate enzymes down to a human-reviewable list?
options: A single filtering script
Agents progressively narrowed the pool: 200,000+ candidates to 3,500 candidate systems to 20 written-up reports
Random sampling
Only enzymes from human pathogens were kept
questions.explanation: The pipeline was a funnel: broad gathering (200,000+), filtering to 3,500 candidate systems, then a final pass to the 20 most compelling, each written up for a human to actually read.

questions.prompt: Why is ART described as a 'lead' rather than a confirmed discovery?
options: Because Anthropic hasn't published anything
Because its function is still unknown and the finding hasn't been independently replicated beyond the pre-print
Because reverse transcriptases don't exist in phages
Because Feng Zhang rejected the finding
questions.explanation: Anthropic states ART's function is unknown; the CRISPR-like resemblance is structural, and the work is reported in a pre-print reviewed — not yet independently replicated — by outside experts like Feng Zhang.
